summary_paragraph: Mr. Johnson, a man with a history of chronic alcohol abuse, atrial fibrillation, and hypertension, was admitted with chest and right-sided abdominal pain. He reported intermittent hematemesis and worsening reflux, with symptoms exacerbated by alcohol use. Initial evaluation revealed atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response, controlled with diltiazem in the ED. Troponins were negative, ruling out acute myocardial infarction. A transthoracic echocardiogram showed moderately depressed left ventricular systolic function with an ejection fraction of 35%, attributed to tachycardia-induced cardiomyopathy. His Diltiazem was discontinued due to heart failure, and he was started on metoprolol succinate, digoxin, and low-dose lisinopril. Liver enzymes were elevated in a pattern consistent with alcohol use, and abdominal pain was thought to be peptic in origin. Despite medical recommendations, the patient demanded discharge, refused to sign AMA paperwork, and eloped from the hospital. Prescriptions and discharge instructions were provided, emphasizing medication adherence and alcohol cessation.
